mainEntity.name: Can flexible dentures be repaired if they crack or break?

acceptedAnswer.text: Flexible dentures can sometimes be repaired, though the process is more specialised than for traditional acrylic dentures. Repairs to thermoplastic materials require specific equipment and techniques, and not all dental laboratories offer this service. In some cases, if the damage is significant or the denture has reached the end of its useful lifespan, replacement may be more appropriate than repair. Your dentist can assess the damage and advise on the best course of action. Attempting home repairs with over-the-counter kits is not recommended, as these products may damage the flexible material further.

mainEntity.name: Can flexible dentures be relined to improve the fit?

acceptedAnswer.text: Relining — the process of adding new material to the fitting surface of a denture to improve its adaptation to the gums — can be more challenging with flexible dentures than with acrylic ones. Some flexible denture systems do allow for relining using compatible materials, but this is not always possible with every brand or in every clinical situation. If your flexible denture feels loose, your dentist can assess whether a reline is feasible or whether a new denture may be the more appropriate solution. Regular reviews help identify fit changes early.

mainEntity.name: Should I wear my flexible dentures at night?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most dental professionals advise removing dentures overnight to allow the gum tissues to rest and recover. Wearing dentures continuously — including during sleep — can increase the risk of fungal infections such as oral thrush and may contribute to irritation of the soft tissues. Removing your denture at night also provides an opportunity to clean it thoroughly. Your dentist can provide specific guidance based on your individual circumstances, as recommendations may vary depending on your oral health and the type of denture you wear.

mainEntity.name: Are flexible dentures suitable for everyone?

acceptedAnswer.text: Flexible dentures are not suitable for every clinical situation. They tend to work well as partial dentures for replacing a smaller number of teeth, particularly where aesthetics and comfort are priorities. However, they may not provide sufficient structural support in cases involving extensive tooth loss, significant bite changes, or where the remaining teeth and gums require a more rigid framework. Conditions such as gum disease or insufficient remaining teeth may also influence suitability. A thorough clinical examination is essential to determine whether flexible dentures are an appropriate option for your particular needs.

mainEntity.name: How much do flexible dentures cost in the UK?

acceptedAnswer.text: The cost of flexible dentures varies depending on the number of teeth being replaced, the complexity of the case, the materials used, and the individual dental practice. As a private dental treatment, pricing is set by each clinic. During a consultation, your dentist can provide a clear treatment plan and cost estimate tailored to your specific requirements. It is worth discussing all available options — including alternative denture types — so that you can make an informed decision that considers both clinical suitability and budget.

Some patients experience a brief adjustment period when first wearing any new denture, during which speech may feel slightly different. This is normal and typically resolves within a few days to a couple of weeks as the tongue and muscles of the mouth adapt to the new appliance. Flexible dentures are generally thinner than some acrylic alternatives, which some patients find helps with speech adaptation. If speech difficulties persist beyond the initial adjustment period, it is advisable to return to your dentist, as a minor adjustment to the denture may help resolve the issue.
